content.title: About
content.content: Puff pastry is a light, flaky dough made from flour, butter, water and salt. During baking the layers separate, creating an airy, crisp texture. It is used in both sweet and savory dishes such as croissants, turnovers, tartlets and dessert pastries.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Puff pastry originated in France in the 17th century and quickly spread across Europe.
Thin layers are created by repeatedly rolling and folding the dough with butter – a process called "lamination".
Depending on the technique, a sheet can contain anywhere from 27 to over 100 layers.
In the United States, ready‑to‑use puff pastry sheets are a common shortcut for pies and appetizers.
The pastry readily absorbs the flavors of its filling, enhancing overall taste.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Puff pastry provides carbohydrates and a modest amount of fat, delivering quick energy.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: The flour and occasional yeast used in the dough supply B1, B2 and niacin, important for metabolism.

items.title: Iron content
items.content: Whole‑grain versions of puff pastry contain iron, which supports blood formation.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Because puff pastry is rich in fats and carbs, it should be eaten in moderation, especially for weight management.

items.title: Trans‑fat presence
items.content: Using margarine instead of butter can introduce trans fats, which are detrimental to heart health.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional puff pastry contains wheat, making it unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Puff pastry can be baked as croissants, turnovers, tarts, used as a base for casseroles or sweet desserts. It is often brushed with egg before baking to achieve a golden crust.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store baked puff pastry in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze in a zip‑lock bag for up to 3 months. Thaw in the refrigerator and let it reach room temperature before baking.
